description: Soy Javier, programador y estudiante de Desarrollo de Software. Trabajo con C#, .NET, APIs y bases de datos. Me interesa usar datos abiertos para resolver problemas reales. En zirocooles queremos aprender juntos y convertir una idea en un prototipo para el NASA Space Apps Challenge. Busco personas con interés o habilidades en desarrollo web, análisis y visualización de datos, diseño UX/UI o comunicación. Si te entusiasma crear en equipo, ¡sumate!🚀
summary:
Mars Base is a bilingual browser game that puts children ages 7–12 in charge of a Martian outpost. Players have six Martian days to keep four astronauts supplied and safe. When a dust storm cuts solar power, they decide whether to use the battery to keep the greenhouse lights on or save energy and delay the harvest. During a solar particle alert, they weigh the benefit of cleaning the panels against the risk of keeping the crew outside while waiting for a reply from Earth.

The alert draws on a historical NASA DONKI record, and the greenhouse design draws on the Canadian Space Agency’s Interplanetary Farming activity. Illustrated previews let players compare what each choice costs before committing. By replaying the mission, children can see how small decisions add up and practice the kind of trade-offs that matter when living far from Earth.
details:
How Mars Base works

Mars Base is a bilingual browser game created for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players ages 7–12 manage a Martian outpost for six sols, or Martian days, and try to keep four astronauts supplied and safe.

Each turn presents a decision with a cost. During a dust storm, players can use the battery to keep the greenhouse lights on or save power and delay the lettuce harvest. When a solar particle alert arrives, they can send the crew into the shelter or keep them outside to clean the panels while waiting for a radio reply from Earth. Before confirming a plan, players see illustrated comparisons of how much battery power, water, and food they have now and how much they would have left. A mission log records what happened so they can compare strategies across playthroughs.

Educational benefit and intended impact

The goal is for children to explain why a decision helped or hurt their mission. A player who saves electricity by recycling less water can see the tank drain faster. A player who postpones panel cleaning to shelter the crew can see how that choice affects the next day’s power supply. The game is designed for independent play or a classroom discussion where students compare their choices and explain what they would do differently.

Data, tools, and design choices

  • Space science. A historical NASA DONKI record inspired the solar alert. NASA’s Opportunity rover observations informed the dust-storm scenario, and NASA’s Earth–Mars communication data informed the radio delay. The Canadian Space Agency’s Interplanetary Farming activity informed the greenhouse and lettuce crop. The app credits these sources and identifies resource costs and radiation points as simplified game values.
  • Development. I built the game with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, used PNG sprite sheets for animation, and published it through GitHub Pages. It runs in a browser without an account, an API key, or specialized hardware.
  • Creative approach. The animations show the consequences of a choice. Players see dust come off the panels, the crew enter the shelter, or the greenhouse lights go out. They can compare two plans before spending any resources.
  • Accessibility. I used short prompts, a small set of choices per turn, and illustrations alongside numbers. The layout adapts to phones, the game respects reduced-motion preferences, and players can switch between Spanish and English without losing their progress.
